title: Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL / bit.ly)
tagline: The classic warm-up: short codes, base62, and a read-heavy system that must redirect in milliseconds.
summary: Base62 short codes, the read-heavy redirect path, caching, scale.

paragraphs: Start by scoping. State functional and non-functional requirements before designing — this is the highest-signal habit.

blocks.title: Functional
items: Given a long URL, produce a short URL.
Visiting the short URL redirects to the original long URL.
(Optional) custom aliases, expiration, basic analytics (click counts).

blocks.title: Non-functional
items: Highly available — a dead redirect breaks every link ever shared.
Very low latency on redirect (the read path is the product).
Short codes are unique and not easily guessable/enumerable.

blocks.text: Immediately flag the defining characteristic: this is an extremely read-heavy system (people create a link once, click it thousands of times). That single observation drives the whole design toward caching and read optimization.

items.detail: 100:1 read:write → ~100,000 redirects/sec. This dominates — cache aggressively.
~500 bytes/record × 100M/day ≈ 50 GB/day → ~18 TB over a year; keep for years → tens of TB. A sharded key-value store handles this easily.
Using base62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9): 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations. 7 characters comfortably covers many years of growth.

codes.title: api

blocks.title: 301 vs 302 redirect
blocks.text: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect → fewer hits to your server (great for load) but you lose per-click analytics and can't change the target. 302 (temporary) routes every click through you → enables analytics and editable targets, at higher load. For an analytics-tracking shortener, use 302.

sections.title: 4. The core problem: generating short codes

paragraphs: The heart of the design is mapping a long URL to a unique short code. Three common approaches:

items.term: Hash the URL (e.g., MD5) and take first N chars
items.detail: Simple, but hashes collide when truncated — you must detect collisions and re-hash, and identical URLs map to the same code (maybe undesirable for analytics). Workable but fiddly.

Maintain a global incrementing counter; encode each new id in base62 to get the short code. Guarantees uniqueness (no collisions), short codes, and is simple. The only challenge is generating unique ids at scale — use a distributed ID generator (Snowflake) or hand out ID ranges to each server from a central allocator.

A separate service pre-generates a large pool of unique random base62 codes into a 'available keys' store; app servers grab unused ones. Decouples key generation from the write path and avoids collisions and sequential/guessable codes.

blocks.title: Why not a plain auto-increment column?
blocks.text: A single auto-increment DB column is a write bottleneck and SPOF, and pure sequential codes are guessable/enumerable (security & privacy issue). Use a distributed ID generator with base62 encoding, or a key-generation service handing out shuffled keys, so codes are unique without a single hot counter.

blocks.caption: Write path creates a code and stores the mapping; read path is cache-first for blazing redirects.

items.title: Shorten (write)
items.detail: Client POSTs long URL → service gets a unique id (distributed ID gen), base62-encodes it to a code, stores `code → longUrl` in the KV store, returns the short URL.

items.title: Redirect (read)
items.detail: Client GETs /{code} → service checks Redis first; on hit, return 302 instantly. On miss, read the KV store, populate the cache, then redirect. Since reads dominate and the hot set is small, cache hit rate is very high.

blocks.title: Why a key-value store
blocks.text: The access pattern is a pure key lookup (code → URL) with no joins or range queries, at huge scale. That's the textbook case for a sharded key-value/NoSQL store (DynamoDB/Cassandra), sharded by the short code via consistent hashing. SQL would work at small scale but the KV pattern + horizontal scale fits perfectly.

items.detail: Redis cache absorbs ~100k reads/sec; add read replicas of the KV store; put popular redirects behind a CDN/edge if appropriate.
Stateless app servers behind an LB; distributed ID generation avoids a central counter bottleneck; shard the KV store by code.
Replicate the KV store across AZs; redundant LBs; the cache is an optimization, not a SPOF (misses fall through to the DB).
Don't write a DB row synchronously on every click (kills the read path). Emit a click event to a queue (Kafka) and aggregate counts asynchronously.
Store a TTL; a background job (or DB TTL feature) purges expired entries lazily.

blocks.text: Tie each scaling move to the read-heavy nature: cache-first redirect, async analytics off the hot path, distributed IDs to avoid a write bottleneck. Finishing with 'the cache is the star here because it's 100:1 reads' shows you internalized the requirements.

cheatsheet: URL shortener is extremely read-heavy → design around caching and a fast key lookup.
Short code = base62-encode a unique id (7 chars → 62^7 ≈ 3.5T); avoid a single auto-increment (bottleneck + guessable).
Generate unique ids via a distributed ID generator (Snowflake) or a key-generation service; not one hot counter.
Store code→URL in a sharded key-value store (pure key access, no joins); cache hot codes in Redis (cache-first redirect).
302 redirect (route every click) for analytics/editable targets; 301 (cacheable) for max performance.
Do click analytics asynchronously via a queue — never write a DB row on the hot redirect path.

questions.prompt: How do you generate unique 7-character short codes at 1,000+ writes/sec across many servers without collisions or a single bottleneck?
questions.hint: Avoid one central counter; think distributed IDs or pre-generated keys.
answer: Two clean approaches. (1) **Distributed ID generation + base62**: use a Snowflake-style generator (or a central allocator that hands each app server a *range* of ids, e.g., 10,000 at a time) so each server mints unique numeric ids locally without contention; base62-encode the id to a 7-char code. Uniqueness is guaranteed because ids never repeat. (2) **Key Generation Service**: a separate service pre-generates a large pool of unique random base62 codes into an 'available' table; app servers atomically claim unused codes. This decouples generation from the write path and yields non-sequential (non-guessable) codes.

Both avoid a single hot counter (which would bottleneck and be a SPOF) and avoid hash collisions. I'd prefer ranges/Snowflake for simplicity, or the key-gen service if non-enumerable codes are a requirement.
keyPoints: Snowflake / ID-range allocation → local unique ids, base62 encode
Or Key Generation Service: pre-generate + claim unused codes
Guarantees uniqueness without collisions or contention
followUps: How would you support custom aliases alongside generated codes without collisions?

questions.prompt: A link goes viral — one short code gets millions of redirects per minute. How does your design hold up, and what would you watch?
questions.hint: It's a single hot key on the read path.
answer: This is a single hot *read* key, which the design handles well: the code→URL mapping for that link sits in Redis and is served from memory, so even millions of redirects/min are cheap memory lookups — the database barely sees them. You can also push that hot redirect to a CDN/edge or replicate the cache to multiple nodes/regions for geographic spread.

What to watch: (1) **cache stampede** if that hot key ever expires — pin/refresh hot keys or use serve-stale-while-revalidate; (2) the **analytics** path — don't synchronously write a DB row per click; emit click events to a queue and aggregate, or you'll create a write hot spot; (3) ensure the cache node holding it isn't itself a bottleneck (replicate/shard the cache). Because it's a read-only hot key, this is far easier than a hot *write* key.
keyPoints: Hot read key served from Redis/CDN — DB barely touched
Replicate/edge-cache the hot mapping for spread
Async analytics so clicks don't create a write hot spot
followUps: How would the answer differ if the hot key were a write (like a counter) instead of a read?
